doc.title: Carmen Leggio interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Chloe's repertoire, packed crowds and the group's breakup
summary: Tunes played at Chloe's, Lester Young in line, 17 weeks of six nights until the owner's unpaid taxes ended it and the players scattered.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. I was just going to ask, I wanted to know, in the Bill Potts Quartet and in this band with Keter, can you name a couple of the songs that would kind of summarize what you were doing at that point?

Yeah. “Flyin’ Home,” “Body and Soul,” these were the things that were happening at that time. “Satin Doll” was still there and “A Train.” All the things that they’re even doing © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

nowadays. And “C Jam Blues.” All those tunes, we used to — the place would be packed. Like I told you we had to break into — Lester Young was in line. There was Shadow Wilson, I don’t know if you remember, they were in line to see us. Around the corner was the Howard Theater, where all the big bands used to come play, and they’d come in and see us. And we had a cooking group. And the reason it broke up, we were there 17 weeks, six nights a week for five hours a night playing hard, I mean playing hard. And the reason it broke up was because the lady that owned the place didn’t pay the taxes. So we broke up and then we all split up, and I came back here to Tarrytown. June Bug came back. Keter stayed down there with Dinah Washington and started playing with Ella Fitzgerald and all that. He stayed in Washington. Louis Derry went back to New Rochelle where he’s still living now. But my friend June Bug passed away in 1959. So that’s part of it.
